title: Sowing leek microgreens
subtitle: How to sow a leek microgreen tray — the slow-starting allium crop
excerpt: Leek microgreens are sown with no pre-treatment, but at a higher seed rate than brassicas to compensate for slower and less even germination. Scatter 25 to 30 g per 25 cm tray, press into the medium, and blackout for four to five days. Germination is noticeably slower than brassica crops.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The characteristic bent shape of germinating allium seedlings (leek, onion, chive). The shoot emerges from the seed in a loop shape before straightening upright. This is normal behaviour; the loop straightens within 24 hours of moving to light. The blackout cover should be removed once most loops have straightened, not before.

The period immediately after sowing when a second tray is stacked on top, blocking light from the sown tray. In darkness, germinating seeds direct energy into pushing the shoot upward rather than greening. For leek, the blackout phase runs four to five days.

content.text: Leek microgreens are sown using the same basic method as brassica microgreens but at a higher seed rate. Leek seed is flat, black, and slightly angular; it scatters less evenly than round brassica seed. Germination takes four to five days rather than two to three, and the blackout cover is removed once the characteristic looped shoots have straightened.

One 25 cm × 25 cm growing tray. A second tray for the blackout cover. Seed compost. Leek seed: 25 to 30 g per tray (higher than most brassica crops to compensate for lower germination rates). A flat piece of card for pressing.
Step 1: pre-dampen seed compost and fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim. Level the surface.

Step 2: scatter leek seed at 25 to 30 g per tray. Leek seed is flat and slightly irregular in shape; scatter from 15 to 20 cm above the tray and work systematically across in sections. The seed is light and can drift; work in a calm area or use your other hand as a windbreak.

Step 3: press firmly into the medium using the flat base of the second tray or a piece of card. Good seed-to-medium contact is more important for leek than for brassicas, as leek seed germinates more slowly and needs consistent moisture access.
: cover with the second tray and a light weight. Leave for four to five days.

: when you first check the tray at day 4, some shoots may still be in the characteristic bent loop shape. This is normal. Replace the cover and check again at day 5; most loops will have straightened. Remove the cover and move to light once the majority are upright.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common sowing-stage problems with leek microgreens.

items.cause: Cold room, old seed, or seed not in contact with the medium.
items.fix: Confirm room temperature is above 16°C. Use fresh leek seed from the current season. Press more firmly on the next attempt.

items.cause: Leeks germinate and develop more slowly than brassicas.
items.fix: Replace the cover and check again at day 7. Shoots will straighten on their own once they are tall enough to do so. Do not force them upright.

items.symptom: Very thin coverage even with higher seed rate
items.cause: Leek seed viability declines after one season.
items.fix: Use fresh seed. Increase the seed rate to 35 g per tray on the next attempt.
